summary.text: 没 is the standardized simplified form of 沒. The common reading méi means “not have”; a contested proposal says the graph was borrowed to write this different word because the words may have sounded alike, while other accounts connect the negative use with 勿, 未, or 有. The sound match and borrowing path remain unverified.

formation.text: The construction of traditional 沒 is disputed. The received 說文 analyzes it as 水 plus 𠬸; later commentary assigns 𠬸 a sound role, while another account describes a hand reaching into water. No inspected early glyph witness resolves these accounts, and the proposed sound component’s reading and historical relation to 沒 are unverified.

history.text: 没 is identified as the standardized simplified form of 沒 and is also classified as a variant. A variant-dictionary account says the right side of a common form was often corrupted into 殳. This supports a corruption account for that variant but does not establish a complete graphic sequence leading to standardized 没. The related 𣳚 is described as stroke-reduced; its cited inscription is undated.

uncertainties.text: The hand-in-water picture and the analysis of 沒 as 水 plus 𠬸 are competing accounts; the graph’s original construction remains unsettled.
Later commentary assigns 𠬸 a sound role, but its reading and historical sound relation to 沒 remain unverified.

The origin and chronology of méi “not have” remain unresolved. One proposal is that the graph used for “sink” or “drown” was borrowed for this different word because the words may have sounded alike; other proposals involve 勿, 未, or 有. No primary evidence establishes the proposed sound match or borrowing path.

senses.text: The received 說文 glosses 沒 as 沈, “sink” or “submerge”; dictionary accounts also record sinking and drowning. These uses are documented, but their earliest attestation and the graph’s original meaning are not established.

Duan Yucai interprets “complete entry into water” as extending to “end” or “exhausted,” citing classical examples. This is his account of a semantic development; the earliest use and chronology are unresolved.

In the common reading méi, 沒 is used for “not have” and “none.” One contested proposal is that the graph used for “sink” or “drown” was borrowed to write this different word because the words may have sounded alike. Other accounts propose connections involving 勿, 未, or 有; the older word’s sound, proposed match, borrowing path, and first use remain unresolved.

limitations.text: The cited examples for “sink” and “end/exhausted” were not independently dated, so earliest attestations remain unresolved.
No primary textual evidence establishes the first use of méi “not have” or the proposed sound-based borrowing path.

overview.text: 没 is the simplified form of 沒, commonly read méi and meaning “not have.” The sound-based borrowing proposed for this negative meaning is contested; the graph’s earlier construction is disputed.

takeaway.text: The proposed borrowing treats “not have” as a different word written with 沒 because the words may have sounded alike; the sound match remains unverified, and other origin proposals exist.

relationships.text: 没 is identified as the standardized simplified form of 沒. A separate account describes corruption of the right side in a common variant but does not establish a complete graphic sequence for standardized 没.
